fuller.text: This report asks whether today's AI systems, or ones built soon, could be conscious. It was written by a group of philosophers, neuroscientists and AI researchers. By "conscious" they mean having subjective experience: there is "something it is like" to be the system, as there is to see a screen or feel pain. Their method is to check AI systems against the best-supported brain-science theories of consciousness.

Their method is to check AI systems against the best-supported brain-science theories of consciousness.

fuller.text: The authors take seriously that conscious AI could be built within the next few decades. Chatbots that imitate human conversation will also likely lead many people to believe some AI is conscious, whether or not it is. Missing real consciousness could mean causing suffering to beings that deserve moral concern. Wrongly seeing it could waste effort better spent on humans and animals, so both kinds of mistake carry costs.

fuller.text: The approach rests on three assumptions. Computational functionalism: running the right kind of computation is enough for consciousness, so the material a system is made of does not matter; they adopt this as a working guess. Scientific theories of consciousness, built mostly from human brain studies, have real evidence behind them and describe functions that AI could also perform. A "theory-heavy" approach, looking at how a system works inside, beats behaviour tests, because AI can be trained to mimic humans while working very differently.

fuller.text: From a survey of theories, the authors draw up 14 "indicator properties": features that make a system more likely to be conscious. They do not pick a winning theory or claim any feature is definitely required. Systems with more indicators are simply better candidates, though some indicators matter more than others. Integrated information theory is left out, because it denies that the right computation alone is enough.

fuller.text: Recurrent processing theory points to information being fed back and processed repeatedly, rather than passing straight through once. Global workspace theory points to specialised parts sharing a small common "workspace" whose contents are broadcast back to all of them. Higher-order theories point to a monitor that judges whether perceptions are reliable or just noise. Other indicators cover agency, meaning learning from feedback to pursue goals, and embodiment, meaning modelling how one's own actions change what one senses.

fuller.text: Next, the authors ask how each indicator could be built. Many already exist: repeated, looping processing is common in standard neural networks. Reinforcement learning, where a system learns by trial and reward, is arguably enough for basic agency. No working system yet clearly meets all four workspace indicators, but the authors argue this is a realistic goal.

fuller.text: They then test real systems. Large language models built on the Transformer design make only a weak case, because information does not loop back and there is no separate workspace. The Perceiver, a design with a small shared memory space, comes closer but lacks broadcast back to all its parts. Of three AIs that control robot or virtual bodies, DeepMind's Adaptive Agent seems most likely to count as embodied by their standard.

fuller.text: The authors name several limits. The indicators are vague enough to need interpretation, and sharper versions would go beyond the evidence. Knowing a system's design and training is sometimes not enough; tools that look inside trained networks may be needed. Human evidence also cannot say how different a process can be while still producing consciousness.

fuller.text: The conclusion: no current AI system appears to be a strong candidate for consciousness. Yet most indicators could be built with existing techniques, so if computational functionalism is true, conscious AI could realistically arrive soon. The authors call for more research on consciousness in AI and urgent thought about the moral risks, which this report leaves aside.

brief.text: This report asks whether AI systems could be conscious: able to have experiences that feel like something. The authors say this matters because AI is improving fast, and chatbots that talk like people may lead many to believe they are conscious. So they judge AI by how it works inside, using brain science theories, not by how it behaves.

brief.text: From those theories they draw a list of indicator properties: signs that make consciousness more likely. Looking at several current systems, they find none is a strong candidate. But they see no obvious technical barrier to building AI with many of these signs. If consciousness depends only on how information is processed, conscious AI could realistically be built soon.
